t: How autism freed me to be myself
w: A short talk by an autistic young woman about how her mind works and how she writes and imagines. Warm, funny and easy to stop after six minutes.
h: One person's account. Autism looks different in different people, so take what fits and leave the rest.

t: This is what it's really like to live with ADHD
w: Jessica McCabe has ADHD and explains it from the inside: why 'just try harder' does not work, what the brain science says, and what helped her. Kind in tone and practical.
h: A personal story with some science, not clinical advice. What worked for her may not work for you.

w: A developmental psychologist shows that even the youngest minds learn by testing ideas, the way a scientist does. A light way into how a mind builds its picture of the world.
h: It is about children, not about autism or ADHD, and it is a popular summary of her lab's work.

t: The world needs all kinds of minds
w: Temple Grandin is autistic. She describes thinking in pictures, how that differs from thinking in words or patterns, and why a world with only one kind of mind would get stuck.
h: She describes her own way of thinking, which is one pattern among autistic people, not all of them. Some of her wider views are debated.

t: You aren't at the mercy of your emotions -- your brain creates them
w: A neuroscientist and psychologist argues that emotions are built by the brain from body signals and past experience, rather than set off like fixed reflexes. Useful for reading a heavy mood as a signal about the body's budget, not a verdict on your life.
h: This is one side of a live scientific debate, and she says so. Treat it as a way of looking, not settled fact.

w: A journalist who wrote a history of autism traces how it was understood, misunderstood and renamed over a century, and why the idea of neurodiversity grew out of it.
h: Given in 2015 by a journalist, not a clinician. Later historical work on Hans Asperger's wartime record complicates the story told about him here.

t: The riddle of experience vs. memory
w: A psychologist who won the Nobel prize in economics explains why the self that lives through a day and the self that remembers it disagree, and what that does to how we judge a life.
h: A 2010 talk. Some of the research behind it is more nuanced than twenty minutes can show.
